topic: rear axle position and chain slack (2019-2022 450 SX-F)
statement: On the 2019-2022 450 SX-F a tester moved the axle from about 608 mm to 595 mm from the swingarm pivot, which gave more front grip out of corners and less squat on acceleration. Being 2-3 mm off is fine, but 10 mm changes the bike's character. Chain slack worked best at 65-68 mm: 60 mm felt harsh, over 68 mm felt disconnected.
notes: Stock gearing; model year not stated (article Sept 2021, so 2021/2022 bike). Measured centre of pivot bolt to centre of axle. For 2025 the same source suggests 600-606 mm (cd6 optional-torque record). Carried to 2019: same platform generation (2019-2022); the statement names the year it was tested or measured on where that matters.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested: KTM 450 SX-F chain and axle position tips

topic: what moving the axle back does
statement: Moving the rear axle back makes the shock feel softer, because the swingarm has more leverage on it, so you may need more compression. It also lengthens the wheelbase and puts more weight on the front tire, which improves high-speed stability but can slow cornering. The 2019 swingarm was 5 mm longer than before.
notes: Written about the 2018.5 Factory Edition and 2019 450 SX-F; the principles apply to any linkage bike. Carried to 2019: same platform generation (2019-2022); the statement names the year it was tested or measured on where that matters.

source.name: Motocross Action: The long and short of moving your KTM axle rearward

statement: Testers often move to a 14T countershaft with a bigger rear sprocket (e.g. 14/52 instead of 13/49) because it settles the rear on acceleration and braking bumps. One rider reports a smaller countershaft adds squat and makes the bike easier to loft or seat-bounce. Small countershafts also wear chains faster, so going one tooth bigger in front and about three bigger at the back is common.

vals.tester_choice: 14T front + bigger rear to calm the rear
vals.small_countershaft: more squat (single rider report), faster chain wear
vals.chain: bigger combo needs a longer chain

notes: The squat effect comes from one poster; most posters said the chain-wear difference is small. Do not use 14T on 2021+ CRF450R (slave cylinder clearance). KTM lowered its countershaft 3 mm in 2023 for the same anti-squat reason. Carried to 2019: same platform generation (2019-2022); the statement names the year it was tested or measured on where that matters.

Testers rated the handling intuitive and the coil fork the best part of the bike.

statement: 2010 CRF450R changes on the 2009 fuel-injected platform: a new EFI map, a redesigned automatic decompressor, fork with new seals, more oil and firmer low-speed compression, a shock with a new piston, high-speed adjuster and valving, and the ECU connector moved behind the radiator shroud. Frame geometry is unchanged.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2010 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2010 CRF450R made 50.90 hp at 8,400 rpm and weighed 226.5 lb, about 10 lb lighter than most of the class. Power is mellow and low-to-mid: best from about 6,000 to 8,200 rpm, flat above 8,000 to the 11,200 rpm limiter.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2010 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2010 CRF450R setup: fork 0.48 kg/mm springs (stock 0.46), 355 cc oil, compression 6 clicks out (stock 13), rebound 8 out, legs flush. Shock stock 5.4 kg/mm spring (riders under 175 lb can go one rate softer), 105 mm sag once the fork is stiffened (115 with stock fork springs), high-speed 2 turns out (stock 1-1/2), low-speed 11 clicks out, rebound 15 out (stock 14). Gearing 13/49 in place of 13/48.

vals.shock: 5.4 kg/mm, sag 105 mm, HSC 2 turns, LSC 11 out, reb 15 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2010 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2009-2012 CRF450R: it can flame out at low rpm (raise the idle; a flywheel weight of about 17 oz helps), the four-spring clutch slips under hard use (remove the judder spring and narrow plate and fit a full-size plate, add stiffer springs, or fit a six-spring aftermarket clutch), the brakes fade with the disc guards on in long motos, the stock 1.1 radiator cap boils over (1.6-2.0 caps were used) and the engine oil has to be checked on a dipstick.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2010 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: The 2009-2012 CRF450R sits low at the front and high at the rear. It oversteers and tucks on turn-in, dives under braking and pushes mid-corner. The cures testers settled on were stiffer fork springs, a longer shock link (lowers the rear about 10 mm) and keeping the steering damper. 2010 measured 96.7 dB, over the 94 dB limit of the time.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2010 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: 2011 CRF450R changes: throttle body reduced from 50 mm to 46 mm, a muffler 100 mm longer with a 26 mm core (was 36 mm), a remapped EFI, a judder spring and stiffer springs in the clutch, a new shock linkage, lighter fork cartridge parts and a steering damper body enlarged from 20 mm to 24 mm.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2011 Honda CRF450 test

statement: The 2011 CRF450R made about 52 hp on a magazine dyno, 1.1 hp more than the 2010. Its best power is from 5,000 to 7,700 rpm and it is flat from there to 11,300 rpm, with a soft hit.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2011 Honda CRF450 test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2011 CRF450R setup: fork 0.49 kg/mm springs (stock 0.46), 355 cc oil, compression 12 clicks out (stock 13), rebound 8 out, legs flush. Shock 5.4 kg/mm spring, 105 mm sag (110-115 if the stock fork springs stay), high-speed 2 turns out (stock 1-1/2), low-speed 14 clicks out, rebound 14 out. Gearing 13/49 in place of 13/48.

vals.fork: comp 12 out, reb 8 out, flush
vals.shock: sag 105 mm, HSC 2 turns, LSC 14 out, reb 14 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2011 Honda CRF450 test

statement: 2012 CRF450R changes: fork springs up to 0.49 kg/mm from 0.46 with 10 cc more oil and stronger lower legs, a new linkage with a softer rate that lowers the rear 5 mm, wider and longer footpegs and Dunlop MX51 tyres. Engine, mapping and exhaust are unchanged. List price was $8,440.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Honda CRF450 test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2012 CRF450R made 52.59 hp, the lowest of the five Japanese and Austrian 450s that year, and weighed 231 lb without fuel, 7-13 lb less than its rivals. Tractable and easy to ride, flat above about 8,600 rpm. An aftermarket exhaust added about 2.5 hp at peak in testing.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Honda CRF450 test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2012 CRF450R setup: fork stock 0.49 kg/mm springs, 365 cc oil, compression 12 clicks out, rebound 9 out, legs flush. Shock 5.4 kg/mm spring, 105 mm sag, high-speed 1 turn out (stock 1-1/2), low-speed 12 clicks out, rebound 13 out. Gearing: 13/49 for novices and vets, 14/52 for faster riders.

vals.fork: 365 cc, comp 12 out, reb 9 out, flush
vals.shock: sag 105 mm, HSC 1 turn, LSC 12 out, reb 13 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Honda CRF450 test

statement: The 2013 CRF450R was a new bike: a frame with main spars 40 mm lower, a shock 14.5 mm shorter mounted lower, twin short mufflers, Kayaba PSF air fork in place of coil springs, exhaust valves up from 30 to 31 mm, compression up from 12.0:1 to 12.5:1, more cam overlap, a stronger gearbox with the same ratios and the return of the six-spring, eight-plate clutch. This platform ran 2013-2016.

vals.fork: Kayaba PSF (air)

source.name: Motocross Action - 2013 Honda CRF450 test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2013 CRF450R made 51.55 hp (2012: 52.59) and weighed 234 lb (2012: 231). It is stronger off the bottom than the old engine but gives up its advantage around 7,000 rpm and is flat past about 8,200-9,000 rpm. It measured 116.1 dB on the two-metre test.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2013 Honda CRF450 test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2013-2014 CRF450R setup: fork air pressure 35 psi (Honda recommended 33 psi for 2013, 35 for 2014), compression 11 clicks out (stock 13), rebound 10 out, legs 5 mm up. Shock 5.7 kg/mm spring (stock 5.5), 100 mm sag, high-speed 2 turns out (stock 1-5/8), low-speed 12 clicks out (stock 14), rebound 8 out. Fork pressure climbs by up to 5 psi during a moto, so bleed or reset between motos.

vals.fork: comp 11 out (stock 13), reb 10 out, 5 mm up
vals.shock: 5.7 kg/mm (stock 5.5), sag 100 mm, HSC 2 turns, LSC 12 out, reb 8 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2013 Honda CRF450 test

statement: On the 2013-2016 CRF450R the countershaft sprocket sits 3 mm further out and the rear hub flange is 3 mm thicker to match. A rear wheel built for the earlier bike, or an aftermarket wheel made to the old spacing, can run the chain out of line and throw it.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2013 Honda CRF450 test

statement: 2014 CRF450R changes: a narrower intake tract, a longer exhaust port divider, a re-aimed injector with split (dual-timing) injection, muffler cores enlarged from 18.5 to 22 mm, a black valve cover, and fork changes (new valving, one-piece rebound piston, oil quantity 242 cc, recommended pressure 35 psi).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Honda CRF450 test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2014 CRF450R peaked at 51.97 hp and made 49.57 hp at 9,900 rpm, where the 2014 YZ450F made 58.22. It weighed 236 lb. Strong roll-on power up to about 8,500 rpm, then flat.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Honda CRF450 test

statement: Stock gearing on the 2013-2016 CRF450R is 13/48 and testers found it tall for the low-to-mid power. They went to 13/49, or 14/52 for a ratio in between.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Honda CRF450 test

statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2013-2016 CRF450R: a spongy clutch that engages close to the grip (replace the judder spring and narrow plate with a full-size plate and add stiffer springs), flame-outs under hard braking (raise the idle a couple of clicks), air-fork seal wear (low-friction seals and fork skins), fork air valves that are hard to reach, a front brake weaker than the class best (oversize disc; remove the disc guard for long motos), and a shock that kicks in braking bumps (stiffer spring and a longer link, which lowers the rear about half an inch). One 2014 test bike had a throttle position sensor fail.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Honda CRF450 test

statement: 2015 CRF450R changes: a revised head, a heat-treated piston, more flywheel inertia, a stronger gearbox, three engine maps on a handlebar button, a shorter exhaust with larger tubes, Kayaba PSF-2 fork (compression in one leg, rebound in the other, high- and low-speed adjusters on the caps), all shock adjusters on the reservoir, a 260 mm front disc and Dunlop MX52 tyres.

vals.fork: Kayaba PSF-2

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Honda CRF450 test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2015 and 2016 CRF450R both peaked at 53.03 hp at 8,500 rpm. Soft right off idle, a broad middle, and flat after about 8,500-8,600 rpm. The 2016 weighed 233 lb.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Honda CRF450 test

statement: The 2015-2016 CRF450R has three maps on a handlebar button: hold it with the engine at low rpm and count the flashes, one for stock, two for mellow, three for aggressive. On the dyno the stock map made 1-2 hp more than the other two everywhere, and testers left it there; the aggressive map is jumpy at first throttle.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Honda CRF450 test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2015 CRF450R setup: fork 35 psi, oil height 92 mm, high-speed compression 14 out (stock 11), low-speed compression 12 out, high-speed rebound 10 out, low-speed rebound 10 out (stock 9), legs 5 mm up. Shock 5.7 kg/mm spring (stock 5.5), 100 mm sag, high-speed compression 19 out, low-speed 15 out, rebound 4 out. Rear sprocket 49 in place of 48. Steering damper turned fully in.

vals.fork: HSC 14 out, LSC 12 out, HSR 10 out, LSR 10 out, 5 mm up
vals.shock: 5.7 kg/mm, sag 100 mm, HSC 19 out, LSC 15 out, reb 4 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Honda CRF450 test

statement: 2016 CRF450R changes: fork 5 mm longer for a slacker head angle, a new rising-rate linkage, a chain roller reduced to 34 mm, adjusters changed from 4 to 8 clicks per turn (so click counts are not comparable with 2015), slightly firmer low-speed compression at both ends and a footpeg bracket with a mud scraper that also fits 2013-2015. No engine changes.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2016 CRF450R setup: fork 35 psi, oil height 87 mm, high-speed compression 24 out (stock 20), low-speed compression 24 out (stock 22), high-speed rebound 25 out (stock 27), low-speed rebound 27 out, legs flush. Shock 56 N/mm spring (stock 54), 105 mm sag, high-speed compression 21 out (stock 19), low-speed 22 out (stock 20), rebound 21 out (stock 22). Use fork high-speed compression for big-hit bottoming and low-speed for everything else.

vals.fork: HSC 24 out, LSC 24 out, HSR 25 out, LSR 27 out, flush
vals.shock: 56 N/mm (stock 54), sag 105 mm, HSC 21 out, LSC 22 out, reb 21 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: The 2017 CRF450R was all new: a finger-follower Unicam head with intake valves 2 mm larger, Showa 49 mm coil-spring fork in place of the air fork, the steering damper dropped, the shock centred and mounted 39 mm lower, shared engine and gearbox oil, a seven-plate clutch, a titanium fuel tank, and new geometry (27.22 degree head angle, 22 mm offset, 4.6 in trail, wheelbase 7 mm shorter). Electric start was an option in 2017. This platform ran 2017-2020.

vals.fork: Showa 49 mm coil spring

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2017 CRF450R setup: fork springs one step stiffer than stock (0.50 against 0.48 kg/mm), compression 10 clicks out (stock 11), rebound 13 out, legs raised to the second line (stock first). Shock 56 N/mm spring (stock 54), 108 mm sag, high-speed compression 3-1/2 turns out, low-speed 12 clicks out, rebound 7 out (stock 10). Rear sprocket 50 in place of 49.

vals.fork: comp 10 out, reb 13 out, second line
vals.shock: 56 N/mm (stock 54), sag 108 mm, HSC 3-1/2 turns, LSC 12 out, reb 7 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: The 2017-2018 CRF450R has three maps on the handlebar button: one blue flash stock, two mellow, three aggressive. The stock map sits between the other two and testers raced it. There is no launch control before 2019.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: The 2017 CRF450R has a jerky, weak change from low to mid, a strong midrange that hooks up, and more top end than the 2016. It weighed 233 lb, the same as the 2016, and measured 119.7 dB on the two-metre test.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: 2018 CRF450R changes: electric start standard with a lithium battery (weight up from 233 to 240 lb), stiffer stock springs (fork 0.48 to 0.50 kg/mm, shock 54 to 56 N/mm), revised maps and thinner, more flexible engine hangers. List price rose $300.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2018 CRF450R setup: fork stock springs, compression and rebound 12 clicks out (pros 10 and 13, vets and novices 13 and 13), legs raised to the second line; 10 cc more oil is the cheap fix for harshness near the bottom of the stroke. Shock stock 56 N/mm spring (light riders 54), 107 mm sag, high-speed compression 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 turns out, low-speed 10 clicks out, rebound 7 out. A shock link 1.5 mm longer than stock was the testers' pick.

vals.fork: comp 12 out, reb 12 out, second line
vals.shock: sag 107 mm, HSC 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 turns, LSC 10 out, reb 7 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2017-2019 CRF450R: the clutch judder spring and plate break and the clutch fades (remove the judder parts and add a full friction plate; add stiffer springs sparingly), the radiator fins dent within about 20 hours and the bike boils over when raced hard (radiator sleeves; a 1.6-2.0 cap in place of the stock 1.1), the front brake is weak at a light pull and grabby when squeezed (better fluid, remove the disc guards), the fork is harsh and dives, and the bike shakes its head on fast rough straights (more sag, around 107-108 mm; some riders refit a steering damper). The airbox side vents let in dirt and water.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: The 2017-2019 CRF450R turns in sharply but is loose mid-corner and at speed, and it is sensitive to front-to-rear balance: small changes in sag or fork height change it a lot. Testers removed the two rear tank bolts and two exhaust-to-subframe bolts to let the frame flex more.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: 2019 CRF450R changes: a reworked exhaust port, a new clutch lifter and pressure plate, twin scavenge pumps, a five-jet piston oil spray, the kickstarter boss removed from the cases, larger mid-pipes, maps by gear using the shift sensor, launch control with three rev settings, revised fork shims, a lighter, more flexible swingarm with a revised linkage, bars mounted 15 mm lower and a larger front caliper piston (30 mm plus 27 mm).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2019 CRF450R peaked at 60.21 hp, the most in the 2019 class (YZ450F 57.51, 450 SX-F 57.14, FC 450 56.40, KX450 55.86, RM-Z450 54.39). It matched the 2018 below 9,000 rpm and gained 2.25 hp at 10,000, 3.0 at 11,000 and 3.4 at 11,600 rpm. It weighed 238 lb and measured 117.5 dB on the two-metre test.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2019 CRF450R setup: fork stock 0.50 kg/mm springs, compression 12 clicks out (pros 8, vets 13), rebound 12 out, legs at the stock height. Shock 56 N/mm spring, 108 mm sag (106-110 tried), high-speed compression 3-1/2 turns out, low-speed 10 clicks out, rebound 7 out. The stock map was preferred; the aggressive map felt crisper but made about 1 hp less everywhere.

vals.fork: comp 12 out (pro 8, vet 13), reb 12 out
vals.shock: sag 108 mm, HSC 3-1/2 turns, LSC 10 out, reb 7 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Honda CRF450 race test

statement: For 2014 the KX450F engine was carried over. Kawasaki had fitted an intake cam with 0.4 mm more lift for 2012 and went back to the lower-lift cam for 2013; the 2014 keeps it. The grips went back to being 10 mm shorter after the longer 2013 grips. Fork is the Kayaba PSF air fork.

vals.fork: Kayaba PSF (air)

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2014 KX450F made 55.05 hp at 9,000 rpm, third in the 2014 class behind the YZ450F and 450 SX-F, but testers rated it the easiest 450 engine to race: smooth off the bottom with a long, even pull through the middle.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: The 2014 KX450F comes with three plug-in couplers: green (stock), black (mellow) and white (aggressive). On the dyno the white coupler showed no peak gain over stock and the black one gave up about 1 hp. Launch control leaves power alone below 7,000 rpm and trims it progressively above, works in first and second and switches off in third. Testers used it on hard dirt and concrete, not in loam.

vals.launch_control: retards above 7,000 rpm, off in 3rd gear

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: Testers added one tooth to the rear sprocket on the 2014 KX450F so third gear could be used sooner out of corners.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: Tester complaints on the 2014 KX450F: the PSF air fork is borderline, the clutch is weak, shifting is notchy under load and the brakes are only average. The backfire screen in the airboot is restrictive and testers removed it. With the bars in the forward mounts the fork air valves are hard to reach, so crossover or rotating air valves were fitted.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: 2015 KX450F changes: bridged-box piston with shorter skirts and a new crown, compression up from 12.5:1 to 12.8:1, a front disc enlarged from 250 mm to 270 mm, Showa SFF-Air TAC (three-chamber) fork replacing the Kayaba PSF, a lighter subframe and a rear axle nut with no cotter pin. The fork is about 2 lb lighter and a 0-300 psi digital pump comes with the bike.

vals.fork: Showa SFF-Air TAC

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX450F test

statement: The 2015 KX450F is smooth off the bottom and strong in the middle; testers felt the 2014 pulled harder down low and faster riders preferred the 2014 powerband. It ranked fourth in the class for peak power.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX450F test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2015 KX450F fork setup: inner chamber 160 psi (stock 145), outer 10 psi (stock 7.5), balance 170 psi (stock 135), compression 9 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 11 out (stock 13), fork legs 5 mm up. They kept the balance pressure above the inner pressure. Readings moved by up to 7 psi between checks with the supplied pump, so check with the same pump every time.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX450F test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2015 KX450F shock setup: stock 5.5 kg/mm spring, 104 mm race sag, high-speed compression 2-1/2 turns out (stock 2), low-speed 9 clicks out (stock 5), rebound 11 out (stock 15).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX450F test

statement: On the 2015 KX450F the stock green coupler pinged under load in testing; the black (mellow) coupler stopped it but cost power, and the white (aggressive) coupler, which testers otherwise preferred, made it worse. Launch control was used on concrete and hardpack starts only.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX450F test

statement: Tester complaints on the 2015 KX450F: pinging and brief cut-outs under power on the stock map, a clutch pack that is marginal for riders who abuse it, a rear brake pedal that needs modifying to run low, and a tall, wide, heavy feel. It measured 120 dB on the AMA two-metre sound test while passing the 94 dB amateur test.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX450F test

statement: The 2012-2015 KX450F chassis is a straight-line bike: tall, very stable at speed and unremarkable in tight turns.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX450F test

statement: The 2016 KX450F was all new and 7.5 lb lighter (4.4 lb from the engine, 3.1 lb from the chassis): thinner cases, cylinder offset 8.5 mm forward, titanium intake valves, intake cam advanced 2 degrees, a direct-linked 43 mm throttle body, a lighter gearbox, a frame with spars 6 mm narrower, a lighter swingarm, a lower 1.66 gal tank, radiators tilted forward 10 degrees (shrouds 1.2 in narrower), Showa SFF-Air TAC fork with thinner inner tubes and a shock spring changed from 53 to 52 N/mm. This platform ran 2016-2018.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2016 KX450F made 55.43 hp (2015: 55.07) with more power from 5,500-7,000 rpm and more over-rev from 9,200-11,300 rpm. It trailed the 2016 450 SX-F by 2.6 hp at 6,000, 1.4 hp at 8,000 and 5.0 hp at 10,000 rpm. It weighed 231 lb on the magazine's scale (2015: about 239 lb).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2016 KX450F fork setup by rider speed: inner chamber 160 psi (vet), 174 (intermediate), 185 (pro); outer 14.5 psi; balance 175 psi (vet), 203 (intermediate and pro); compression 13 clicks out, rebound 13 out, fork legs 5 mm up. Keeping the balance chamber higher than the inner chamber let the fork ride lower and turn better.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2016 KX450F shock setup: stock 52 N/mm spring, 105 mm race sag, high-speed compression 2-1/4 turns out (stock 1-3/4), low-speed 15 clicks out (stock 13), rebound 11 out (stock 12). Stock gearing was kept.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: The 2016 KX450F pinged and popped on deceleration on the stock map; the black (mellow) coupler was the only one that removed the decel pop in testing. Kawasaki's handheld calibration tool (about $700, stores up to 200 maps, seven presets, works on KX models back to 2009) did not cure it either. Launch control works in first and second and drops out in third.

vals.tool: KX FI Calibration Kit, about $700, 200 maps

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2016-2018 KX450F: the stock clutch slips under hard use (fit stiffer clutch springs first), the chain guide and buffer wear fast (an aftermarket guide lasts much longer), the airbox side vents let in water and dirt (tape them when washing), the rear brake pedal is hard to set low without dragging (shorten the master cylinder pushrod thread), and on 2016 bikes the radiator shrouds cracked and the seat base flexed.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: The 2016 KX450F turns far more willingly than the 2015 thanks to the lower weight, flatter seat and narrower tank, but testers found the front loose on corner entry. The footpegs can be lowered 5 mm.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: 2017 KX450F changes: richer mapping at small throttle openings (removes the 2016 ping and decel pop), new triple clamps with a bottom clamp 2.5 mm thicker (49.5 mm), softer fork valving with lower recommended air pressures, the fork-cap air valves swapped over, linkage pull rods 0.5 mm longer, a lighter shock spring at the same rate, a stiffer seat base and in-mould shroud graphics. Engine hardware is unchanged.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2017 KX450F made 55.76 hp at 9,000 rpm and weighed 231 lb. It has a strong middle and signs off past about 9,000 rpm, so it is best ridden a gear high and shifted early. At 10,000 rpm it is about 3 hp down on most rivals and by 11,000 rpm about 10 hp down on the Honda and Yamaha.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2017-2018 KX450F fork setup by rider speed: inner chamber 138 psi (vet), 152 (intermediate), 167 (pro); outer 16.5 psi; balance 160 psi (vet), 174 (intermediate), 189 (pro); compression 13 clicks out, rebound 12 out, fork legs 5 mm up. Balance pressure is kept above inner pressure so the fork rides lower and turns.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2017-2018 KX450F shock setup: stock 52 N/mm spring, 105 mm race sag, high-speed compression 2-1/4 turns out (stock 2), low-speed 15 clicks out (stock 13), rebound 11 out (stock 13).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: The 2016 KX450F pushed and wagged on corner entry; for 2017 the softer fork (more dive) and stiffer clamps made the steering noticeably more accurate. Stock tyres are Bridgestone 403/404 and testers rated them well.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: The 2018 KX450F is the 2017 bike with new graphics; nothing mechanical changed. It was the third year of the 2016 platform and the last KX450F with a kickstarter and the air fork.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: At 231 lb the 2018 KX450F was 8 lb lighter than the YZ450F and 9 lb lighter than the CRF450R on a magazine scale, and 9 lb heavier than the electric-start 450 SX-F. Its air fork is about 3 lb lighter than a comparable coil fork. A little decel pop remains, a sign it still runs slightly lean.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Kawasaki KX450F race test

statement: The 2019 KX450 was all new: finger-follower valve train, intake valves 4 mm larger and exhaust valves 2 mm larger, a plain-bearing big end, a throttle body 1 mm larger with a 12-hole injector, a head pipe 105 mm longer, electric start with a lithium battery, a hydraulic clutch, a Showa coil-spring fork in place of the air fork, a 25 mm front axle (was 20 mm), a 250 mm rear disc (was 240 mm) and footpegs 5 mm wider and 3 mm further back.

vals.fork: Showa coil spring

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX450 race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2019 KX450 made 55.3 hp at 9,500 rpm against 56.4 hp at 8,800 rpm for the 2018. The 2018 made about 1 hp more from 6,000-9,000 rpm and about 1.5 lb-ft more torque from 5,000-9,400 rpm; the 2019 made about 3 hp more at 11,000 rpm. It weighed 233 lb, 2 lb more than the 2018, and feels quick-revving and very responsive off the bottom with its strongest pull above 9,400 rpm.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2019 KX450 fork setup: stock 5.0 N/mm springs are soft for aggressive riders; vets ran an effective 5.1 (one 5.0 and one 5.2 spring), fast riders the optional 5.2, light riders stock. Compression 14 clicks out, rebound 12 out, fork legs up to 2 mm up. Light or slower riders added oil in 5 cc steps to both legs to stop bottoming.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX450 race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2019 KX450 shock setup: stock 54 N/mm spring (52 N/mm for riders under 150 lb), 105 mm race sag, high-speed compression 1-1/4 turns out, low-speed 18 clicks out, rebound 12 out.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX450 race test

statement: On the 2019 KX450 the green (stock) coupler was the strongest overall in dyno testing. Black softens response everywhere and gives up 1-2 hp from 6,000-11,500 rpm. White makes the same peak power as green with a crisper, more aggressive feel.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX450 race test

statement: Tester findings on the 2019 KX450: the clutch slips and fades (fit stiffer springs; some crews remove the judder spring and narrow plate and run a full set of standard plates), the rear brake is grabby (grind a lead-in chamfer on the pads; shorten the pushrod thread for more pedal range), the bottom chain roller wears fast (the KX250 twin-bearing roller fits), the battery's thermal switch can refuse to crank a hot bike until it cools, and a 1.1 radiator cap boiled over in hot racing (a 1.8 or 2.0 cap cured it).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX450 race test

statement: The 2019 KX450 turns sweetly once the fork is kept from diving through its mid-stroke. Testers preferred the footpegs in the lower (5 mm down) position. Stock tyres changed to Dunlop MX3S. The exhaust passes both the amateur and two-metre sound tests.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX450 race test

statement: 2014 KX250F changes: a handlebar launch-control button (retards ignition in first and second), gearbox dogs increased from three to four with new shift-fork grooves, a countershaft sprocket held by a nut and washer instead of a clip, engine mount plates thinned from 4.5 mm to 3.2 mm, revised fork and shock damping and grips 10 mm shorter. The 48 mm Showa SFF (single-spring) fork has been on the bike since 2011 and the dual-injector engine (second injector upstream, feeding from about 7,000 rpm) carries over.

vals.fork: Showa SFF 48 mm (one spring leg, one damping leg)
vals.injectors: two; upstream one comes in near 7,000 rpm

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2014 KX250F made 41.14 hp at 12,200 rpm and 20.36 lb-ft, the same as the 2013. It is quick-responding and broad; the 2014 250 SX-F made more peak power, and pros wanted more top end from the Kawasaki.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2014 KX250F fork setup: stock 0.97 kg/mm spring, preload 15 clicks in (stock 7; four clicks equal 1 mm), compression 8 clicks out (stock 9), rebound 11 out (stock 12), fork legs 5 mm up. Oil quantity 300 cc in the left leg and 223 cc in the right.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2014 KX250F shock setup: stock 5.4 kg/mm spring (suits riders over about 170 lb), 100 mm race sag (stock recommendation 104), high-speed compression 1-1/2 turns out (stock 2), low-speed 10 clicks out (stock 12), rebound 10 out (stock 12).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: The 2014-2016 KX250F comes with three plug-in couplers by the head tube: green (standard), white (soft terrain, more ignition advance, sharper) and black (hard or slick terrain, less wheelspin). Magazine testers raced the white one. Launch control works in first and second and switches off in third; testers found it muted the 250 off the line and did not use it.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2014-2016 KX250F: it resists upshifting under full load (use the clutch or breathe the throttle), the clutch slips after a few hard rides (stiffer springs or an aftermarket clutch), the chain guide wears fast (an aftermarket guide lasts), the fork guards are fragile, the clutch-side grip is vulcanised to the bar, and the rear wallows under power (a longer link pull rod stiffens the first part of the stroke and lowers the rear).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: The 2014-2016 KX250F understeers: the front pushes when it is ridden hard into turns and the bike feels upright. Raising the fork in the clamps helps a little. The two changes testers found that really worked were 22 mm offset triple clamps in place of the stock 22.5 mm and a longer shock link pull rod.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2014 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: 2015 KX250F changes: bridged-box piston, a head pipe with a resonance chamber and the KX450F's larger muffler (to meet the 94 dB amateur limit), a heavier 9.5 kg-cm2 flywheel (8.5 and 9 optional), a 270 mm front disc (was 250 mm), revised SFF valving with coated inner tubes, firmer shock settings, lighter thin-wall axles, a self-locking rear axle nut, a four-position upper clamp (bars 25 mm forward, 15 mm forward, standard or 10 mm back) and footpeg brackets that can be lowered 5 mm.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2015 KX250F fork setup: stock 9.6 N/mm spring (9.2 and 10.0 optional), preload 25 clicks in (stock 8; the adjuster has 40), compression 6 clicks out (stock 7), rebound 11 out (stock 10), fork legs 5 mm up. Set preload and fork height to balance the bike against the shock before touching the clickers.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2015 KX250F shock setup: stock 53 N/mm spring (47, 49, 51 and 55 optional; stock suits riders over about 170 lb), 100 mm race sag, high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed 8 clicks out (stock 11), rebound 13 out (stock 14).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F test

statement: The 2016 KX250F is the 2015 bike with a green rear fender, stronger bearing retainer screws and new graphics. It was the last year of this generation.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2016 KX250F made 39.87 hp and weighed 226 lb, 5 lb more than the 250 SX-F and YZ250F of that year. The engine is broad and instant, about 40 hp across a usable range, against roughly 44 hp for the Austrian 250s.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2016 KX250F setup for a fast rider: fork 9.6 N/mm spring, preload backed fully out (stock 8 clicks in), compression 15 clicks out (stock 7), rebound 10 out, legs 5 mm up; vets and novices went fully out on compression and some took 10 cc of oil out of the left leg. Shock 53 N/mm spring, 100 mm sag, high-speed 2 turns out, low-speed 11 clicks out, rebound 14 out. The front brake went spongy in the first hour and was cured by fresh fluid.

vals.fork: preload full out, comp 15 out, reb 10 out, 5 mm up
vals.shock: sag 100 mm, HSC 2 turns, LSC 11 out, reb 14 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2016 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: The 2017 KX250F was all new and 5 lb lighter (221 lb without fuel, engine 1.75 lb lighter): cylinder leaned forward 7 degrees instead of 14 and offset, a plain-bearing big end, bridged-box piston 6 g lighter, titanium valves, a lighter flywheel, a frame 1.3 in narrower at the shrouds, a lighter swingarm, a link 1 mm longer, the KX450F's stiffer lower clamp, a 9.8 N/mm SFF fork spring (was 9.6) with thicker inner tubes, a flatter seat with the filler 20 mm lower and Dunlop MX3S tyres. Only one airbox vent is real; the right-hand one is blanked. This platform ran 2017-2019.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: On a magazine dyno the 2017 KX250F peaked at 40.06 hp (2017 YZ250F 40.93, Austrian 250s about 44) and revved to 13,400 rpm. Against the 2016 it was equal or down from 6,000-9,300 rpm, about 1 hp up from 9,500-11,500 rpm and softer off the bottom, so it can lose a bike length out of a turn and needs clutch if shifted early.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2017 KX250F setup: fork 9.8 N/mm spring, preload 6 clicks in (stock 8), compression 16 clicks out (stock 8), rebound 15 out (stock 16), standard height; the stock compression setting is stiff, so keep going out until it works. Shock 52 N/mm spring, 105 mm sag, high-speed 2-1/2 turns out, low-speed 10 clicks out (stock 11), rebound 9 out (stock 10); riders over 185 lb add compression. A slight oversteer was tuned out with a few clicks of fork preload.

vals.fork: preload 6 in, comp 16 out, reb 15 out
vals.shock: sag 105 mm, HSC 2-1/2 turns, LSC 10 out, reb 9 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: On the 2017 KX250F testers replaced the green (stock) coupler with the white one: slightly softer right off the bottom but stronger from the middle up. The black coupler was judged too mellow to be useful.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2017 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: 2018 KX250F changes: the downstream injector re-angled from 45 to 30 degrees, fuel pressure up 17%, an intake 20 mm shorter, a longer intake port divider, a new cam with timing advanced from 110 to 106 degrees, a head pipe 3 mm larger and 30 mm longer, new ECU settings, a softer 9.4 N/mm fork spring (was 9.8) with more preload and new valving, and new shock valving. It gained about 3 hp from the bottom through the middle.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: A magazine test crew's 2018-2019 KX250 setup: fork 9.4 N/mm spring, preload 6 clicks in (stock 11), compression 18 clicks out (stock 8), rebound 14 out (stock 16), standard height. Shock 52 N/mm spring (a 49 or 48 N/mm for riders around 130-150 lb), 105 mm sag, high-speed 2-1/2 turns out (stock 2-1/4), low-speed 10 clicks out (stock 11), rebound 9 out (stock 12); over 185 lb add compression. The fork has a harsh spot in the mid-stroke that clickers only partly hide; a revalve cures it.

vals.fork: preload 6 in (stock 11), comp 18 out (stock 8), reb 14 out (stock 16)
vals.shock: sag 105 mm, HSC 2-1/2 turns, LSC 10 out, reb 9 out

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: Stock rear sprocket on the 2018-2019 KX250 is 50 teeth. Racers went to 51 for more drive off turns at the cost of more shifting; play riders stay stock.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: On the 2018-2019 KX250 the green (stock) map is flat off the bottom with good top end, the white (lean) map adds low and mid but signs off sooner, and the black (rich) map is mellow for slick tracks. The best result in testing was a custom map from Kawasaki's calibration tool (about $700, or done by a dealer): leave the stock map alone above 40% throttle and add ignition advance and lean the fuel between 10% and 30% throttle. That also removed the decel pop many of these bikes have.

vals.custom: advance and lean 10-30% throttle, stock above 40%

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Kawasaki KX250F race test

statement: The 2019 KX250 (the F was dropped from the name) is the 2018 bike with new graphics. It is kickstart only, weighs 221 lb and listed at $7,749, the lowest price in the class. The all-new engine came for 2020.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX250 race test

statement: The 2018-2019 KX250 makes about 40 hp, roughly 4 hp less than the Austrian 250s. It builds slowly off the bottom, has a bump in the middle and keeps pulling without falling off; riders often needed two downshifts into a corner where other 250s need one.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX250 race test

statement: Repeated tester findings on the 2017-2019 KX250F/KX250: the clutch fades (stiffer springs first; a full aftermarket clutch for hard users), the chain guide wore out in about 15 hours (use an aftermarket guide rather than another stock one), the right radiator shroud can snap if a boot catches it, the rear brake pedal has little range for riders who run it low, and the blanked right airbox vent can be opened up.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2019 Kawasaki KX250 race test

statement: The 2017-2019 KX250F chassis is slim, light and balanced: it tracks straight, goes into corners precisely and holds a rut, a big step from the 2016. The 2018-2019 fork rides higher and is harsher in braking bumps than the 2017 setting. Bars and pegs adjust for taller riders; shorter riders found the seat tall.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Kawasaki KX250F race test
